paragraph: Welcome to math class! In this course, you will work with classmates and use mathematical practices to make sense of and solve problems. This chapter will introduce you to some of the mathematical concepts that you will learn throughout the course. In previous courses, you may have learned about relationships between two quantities that could be graphed with a straight line. In this chapter, you will first make sense of different representations of functions and the relationship between input and output values. Then, you will explore nonlinear functions and investigate the graphs of various functions to identify key characteristics of the functions. You will also learn a new notation for writing functions and explore the attributes of functional relationships. While you are learning these mathematical ideas, you will develop ways to share your mathematical knowledge with a team as you work together to solve problems. In Chapter 1, you will be introduced to all of the major conceptual ideas of this math course, which include Structures, Proof, and Reasoning; Modeling, Application, and Problem Solving; Transformations, Representation, and Equivalence; and Analysis, Inference, and Variability.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
ABSOLUTE VALUE
Absolute value is the numerical value of a number without its sign. The symbol for absolute value is two vertical bars, | |, one on each side of the number. Absolute value can represent the distance on a number line between a number and 0. Since a distance is always positive, the absolute value is always either a positive value or 0. The absolute value of a number is never negative.
For example, the number −3 is 3 units away from 0, as shown on the number line. Therefore, the absolute value of −3 is 3. This is written |−3| = 3.
Likewise, the number 5 is 5 units away from 0. The absolute value of 5 is 5, written |5| = 5.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings: FAMILIES OF FUNCTIONS. Functions can be categorized into “families.” Linear functions make up a family of functions that change by the same amount over equal intervals. For example, if y increases by 4 over the interval 5 ≤ x ≤ 7, it will also increase by 4 over any equal x-interval, such as 6 ≤ x ≤ 8 and 9 ≤ x ≤ 11. The graphs of linear functions are straight lines. Lines may or may not pass through the origin, and may increase, decrease, or remain horizontal from left to right. Exponential functions make up a family of functions that change by equal factors over equal intervals. For example, if y increases by a factor of 9 over the interval 5 ≤ x ≤ 7, it will increase by a factor of 9 over the intervals 6 ≤ x ≤ 8 and 9 ≤ x ≤ 11. The graphs of exponential functions increase (or decrease) rapidly. The growth of infected people in the “Flu Epidemic” (in problem 1-11) is exponential.
label: NA
reasoning: This is a standard expository math toolkit/definition entry explaining linear and exponential families of functions, with no mention of student errors, misconceptions, or contrasting approaches.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings (continued): A special case of functions in the linear family are direct variation functions (also known as directly proportional). Direct variation functions are linear and their graphs pass through the origin. Direct variation functions represent proportional situations. For instance, if the x-value is doubled (or tripled), the y-value is also doubled (or tripled). The data you gathered in the “Sign on the Dotted Line” lab (in problem 1-11) is an example of an increasing direct variation function. An example of a decreasing direct variation function is the elevation of a submarine descending at a constant speed. Inverse variation functions (also called inversely proportional) make up a family of functions in which y varies inversely to x. That means, for example, when x doubles, y halves; and when x triples, y is divided by 3. The data collected in the “Patio Design” lab (in problem 1-11) is an example of inverse variation. Inverse variation functions will be studied in greater depth in future courses. The term “function” will be defined later in this chapter. Linear functions and exponential functions will be developed in more depth later in this course.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

FUNCTIONS
A relationship between inputs and outputs is a function if there is exactly one output for each input. The following table and graph are representations of the same function.

Input (x): −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Output (y): 16, 9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9

The equation of this function can be written y = (x – 2)^2. The value of y depends on the value of x, so y is called the dependent variable and x is called the independent variable.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings continued from previous page.

Another way to write the equation of a function is by using the notation “f(x) =” instead of “y =”. The function named “f” has input x and output f(x). The graph of y = f(x) is the set of all points of the form (x, f(x)).

In the example, f(5) = 9. When the input is 5, the output is 9. This is read as, “f of 5 equals 9.”

The set of all inputs for which there is an output is called the domain. The set of all possible outputs is called the range. In the previous example, notice that you can input any x-value into the function and get an output. The domain of this function is “all real numbers” because any number can be an input. The outputs are all greater than or equal to 0. The range is y ≥ 0.

The equation x^2 + y^2 = 4 does not represent a function because there are two y-values (outputs) for some x-values, as shown.

paragraph: 2-14. The triangle in the previous problem is called a slope triangle. Slope is a measure of the rate of change, which is seen on a graph as the steepness of a line. paragraph: Methods & Meanings: THE SLOPE OF A LINE. The slope of a line is the ratio of the vertical distance to the horizontal distance of a slope triangle formed by two points on a line. The vertical part of the triangle is called Δy (read “change in y”), while the horizontal part of the triangle is called Δx (read “change in x”). Note that “Δ” is the Greek letter delta, which is often used to represent a difference or a change. Slope indicates both how steep the line is and its direction, upward or downward, when viewed from left to right. It can be written as vertical change / horizontal change or Δy / Δx. Note that lines pointing upward when viewed from left to right have positive slope, while lines pointing downward when viewed from left to right have negative slope. A horizontal line has zero slope, while a vertical line has undefined slope. To calculate the slope of a line, pick two points on the line, draw a slope triangle (as shown in the example), determine Δy and Δx, and then write the slope ratio. You can verify that your slope correctly resulted in a negative or positive value based on its direction. In the given example, Δy = 2 and Δx = 5, so the slope is 2/5.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
LETTERS IN MATHEMATICS
Letters are used in math in various ways, but they do not all represent the same thing. Here are five ways you may see letters used in this course.
1. Unknowns are letters that stand for a specific number that is not known yet. They are used in equations that are being solved.
For example, p is an unknown in the equation 3 + p = 5; p is a number that is not known yet, but it can be figured out.
2. Variables are letters that represent quantities that can change. They can take on different values while maintaining a particular relationship.
For example, x and y are variables in the equation 3 + x = y; as x changes, y changes, too.
3. Constants are letters that stand for fixed, unchanging values. They never vary within a problem or situation. Parameters are constants within specific problems or situations, but when parameters are letters, they can define a whole class of things, such as families of functions.
For example, the number π ≈ 3.14159… is a constant. π is a Greek letter used for the universal mathematical constant that represents the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter. The value of π is always the same, no matter the circle.
Additionally, m and b are parameters in the equation y = mx + b; within a specific problem, m and b will have fixed values, such as −5 and 1, respectively, in y = −5x + 1. Yet, different values of m and b will yield different lines.
4. Labels are letters used as shortcuts for the purpose of naming or identifying. They do not represent a numerical value that changes or is solved for.
For example, f is a label in the equation f(x) = 2x + 3; the name of this function is f. (Note that this equation also has variables: x is the independent variable, and f(x), which represents the output of the function and is sometimes replaced with y, is the dependent variable.)
5. Placeholders are letters that represent values in general examples or rules. These are helpful when discussing properties that are true for a whole collection of values or when generalizing patterns.
For example, a is a placeholder in the property a^(−1) = 1/a; the letter a is used as a placeholder for any non-zero number.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
x- AND y-INTERCEPTS
Recall that the x-intercept of a line is the point where the graph crosses the x-axis (where y = 0). The coordinates of the x-intercept are (x, 0). To calculate the x-intercept, substitute 0 for y and solve for x.
The graph of 2x + 6y = 6 is a line, as shown. The x-intercept is (3, 0).
2x + 6y = 6
2x + 6(0) = 6
2x = 6
x = 3
Similarly, the y-intercept of a line is the point where the graph crosses the y-axis, which happens when x = 0. The coordinates of the y-intercept are (0, y). To calculate the y-intercept, substitute 0 for x and solve for y.
The graph of 2x + 6y = 6 is shown. The y-intercept is (0, 1).
2x + 6y = 6
2(0) + 6y = 6
6y = 6
y = 1

Methods & Meanings
STEP FUNCTIONS
A step function is a special kind of piecewise function (a function composed of parts of two or more functions). A step function has a graph that is a series of line segments that often looks like a set of steps. Step functions are used to model real-world situations where there are abrupt changes in the output of the function.
The endpoints of the segments on step functions are either open circles (indicating that this point is not part of the segment) or filled-in circles (indicating that this point is part of the segment).
The graph shown models a situation in which a tour bus company has buses that can each hold up to 20 passengers, with 5 available buses.

paragraph: PROPERTIES OF REAL NUMBERS: The tile moves have mathematical names, called the properties of real numbers. Commutative Property: The order in which numbers or terms are added or multiplied is not important (e.g., a + b = b + a, a · b = b · a; non-examples: 7 - 2 ≠ 2 - 7, 50 ÷ 10 ≠ 10 ÷ 50). Associative Property: The grouping of numbers or terms being added or multiplied is not important (e.g., (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), (a · b) · c = a · (b · c); non-examples: (5 - 2) - 3 ≠ 5 - (2 - 3), (12 ÷ 4) ÷ 2 ≠ 12 ÷ (4 ÷ 2)). Identity Property of Addition: Adding zero to any expression gives the same expression (e.g., a + 0 = a; non-examples: 5a · 0 ≠ 5a). Identity Property of Multiplication: Multiplying any expression by one gives the same expression (e.g., 1 · a = a; non-examples: 6 + 1 ≠ 6). Additive Inverse Property: For every number a, there is an opposite number −a such that a + (−a) = 0. The sum of additive inverses is zero (e.g., 3 + (−3) = 0; non-examples: 8 − (−8) ≠ 0). Multiplicative Inverse Property: For every nonzero number a, there is a reciprocal number 1/a such that a · 1/a = 1. The product of multiplicative inverses is 1 (e.g., 6 · 1/6 = 1; non-examples: −3/5 + (−5/3) ≠ 1).

paragraph: THE DISTRIBUTIVE PROPERTY: The Distributive Property states that for any three terms a, b, and c, a(b + c) = ab + ac. When a multiplies a group of terms, such as (b + c), then it multiplies through to each term in the group. Examples: −5(12 + (−8)) = (−5)(12) + (−5)(−8); 7(4 − 22) = (7)(4) + (7)(−22); 2x(3x + 4y) = (2x)(3x) + (2x)(4y). The same result can be seen using the following visual methods: ALGEBRA TILES: 2x(3x + 4y) = 6x^2 + 8xy; GENERIC RECTANGLE: 2x(3x + 4y) = 2x · 3x + 2x · 4y = 6x^2 + 8xy.

paragraph: LINEAR EQUATIONS FROM SLOPE AND/OR POINTS: There are many ways to write an equation for a line in y = mx + b form. If you know the slope, m, and y-intercept, b, of a line, you can write the equation of the line directly as y = mx + b. For example, consider a line with a slope of −2/7 and a y-intercept of (0, −8): Known information: m = −2/7, (0, −8). Substitute the known information: y = mx + b => y = −2/7 x − 8. If you know the slope and one point on the line, you can rewrite y = mx + b with the known slope and substitute the coordinates of the known point for x and y. Then solve for b and write the new equation. For example, consider a line with a slope of −4 that passes through the point (5, 30): Known information: (5, 30), m = −4. Substitute and solve for b: y = mx + b => 30 = (−4)(5) + b => 30 = −20 + b => 50 = b. Similarly, you can write the equation of the line when you know two points. First, use the two points to calculate the slope. Then substitute the known slope and either of the known points into y = mx + b. Solve for b and write the new equation. For example, consider a line that passes through the points (3, 7) and (9, 9): Known information: (3, 7), (9, 9). Calculate the slope: Δy = 2, Δx = 6 => m = Δy/Δx = 2/6 = 1/3. Substitute and solve for b: y = mx + b => 7 = (1/3)(3) + b => 7 = 1 + b => 6 = b. Write the equation: m = 1/3, b = 6 => y = 1/3 x + 6.

paragraph:
METHODS & MEANINGS: USING GENERIC RECTANGLES TO MULTIPLY

A generic rectangle can be used to calculate products because it helps to organize the different areas that make up the total rectangle. For example, to multiply (2x + 5)(x + 3), a generic rectangle can be set up and completed as shown. Notice that each product in the generic rectangle represents the area of that part of the rectangle.

(2x + 5)(x + 3) = 2x^2 + 11x + 15
area as product = area as sum

Note that while a generic rectangle helps organize the problem, its size is not to scale. Some students find it helpful to write the dimensions on both pairs of opposite sides of the rectangle.

paragraph:
MAKE SENSE OF PROBLEMS AND PERSEVERE IN SOLVING THEM

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might use concrete objects or pictures to help them conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, “Does this make sense?” They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

paragraph:
REASON ABSTRACTLY AND QUANTITATIVELY

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize: to abstract a given situation, represent it symbolically, and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents; and the ability to contextualize: to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meanings of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

paragraph:
CONSTRUCT VIABLE ARGUMENTS AND CRITIQUE THE REASONING OF OTHERS

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

paragraph:
MODEL WITH MATHEMATICS

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, recognizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts, and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

paragraph:
USE APPROPRIATE TOOLS STRATEGICALLY

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

paragraph:
ATTEND TO PRECISION

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely with others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. paragraph:
LOOK FOR AND MAKE USE OF STRUCTURE

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Early on, for example, students might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 is equivalent to the often well-remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, which prepares them to learn about the Distributive Property. In the expression x^2 + 9x + 14, mathematically proficient students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 − 3(x − y)^2 as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

paragraph:
LOOK FOR AND EXPRESS REGULARITY IN REPEATED REASONING

Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
THE EQUAL VALUES METHOD
The Equal Values Method is a method for solving a system of equations. To use the Equal Values Method, take two expressions that are each equal to the same variable and set those expressions equal to each other. For example, solve the system of equations shown.
2x + y = 5
y = x − 1
Solve the first equation for y. The two equations are now y = –2x + 5 and y = x − 1.
2x + y = 5
−2x   −2x
y = −2x + 5
Then, take the two expressions that equal y and set them equal to each other. Then solve this new equation for x, as shown.
−2x + 5 = x − 1
−3x = −6
x = 2
Once you have determined the value of x, substitute that value into either of the original equations to solve for y. In this example, the second equation is used. In the following example, the first equation is used.
x = 2 -> y = −2x + 5 -> y = −2(2) + 5 -> y = 1
The solution is x = 2 and y = 1, which can be written as the ordered pair (2, 1).
Check the solution by substituting the values of x and y in both of the original equations to verify that they are both true.
y = x − 1 => 1 = 2 − 1 => 1 = 1 (true)
y = −2x + 5 => 1 = −2(2) + 5 => 1 = 1 (true)
label: NA
reasoning: This is a standard reference box explaining the Equal Values Method with a fully worked example and verification steps. There is no error analysis or warning about common mistakes.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
DESCRIBING ASSOCIATION
An association (relationship) between two numerical variables can be described by its form, direction, strength, and outliers.
The shape of the pattern is called the form of the association: linear or nonlinear. The form can be made of clusters of data.
If one variable increases as the other variable increases, the direction is said to be a positive association. If one variable increases as the other variable decreases, there is said to be a negative association. If there is no apparent pattern in the scatter plot, then the variables have no association.
Strength is a description of how much scatter there is in the data away from the trend line. Consider the following examples: NEGATIVE LINEAR ASSOCIATION, NEGATIVE NONLINEAR ASSOCIATION, POSITIVE LINEAR ASSOCIATION WITH CLUSTERS, STRONG NEGATIVE ASSOCIATION, MODERATE NEGATIVE ASSOCIATION, WEAK POSITIVE ASSOCIATION.
An outlier is a piece of data that does not seem to fit into the overall pattern. There is one obvious outlier in the scatter plot shown.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
THE SUBSTITUTION METHOD
The Substitution Method is a way to change two equations with two variables into one equation with one variable. It is convenient to use when one equation is already solved for a variable.
For example, the Substitution Method can be used to solve the following system.
x = −3y + 1
4x − 3y = –11
Use substitution to rewrite the two equations as one. In other words, replace x in the second equation with (−3y + 1) from the first equation to get 4(−3y + 1) − 3y = −11. This equation can then be solved for y, as shown.
4(−3y + 1) − 3y = −11
−12y + 4 − 3y = −11
−15y + 4 = −11
−15y = −15
y = 1
To determine the solution to the system, substitute the value you calculated into either original equation to calculate the other value.
In the example, substitute y = 1 into x = −3y + 1.
x = −3(1) + 1
x = −3 + 1
x = −2
Then write the answer for x and y as an ordered pair: (−2, 1).
To check the solution, substitute x = −2 and y = 1 into both of the original equations.
x = −3y + 1 => −2 = −3(1) + 1 => −2 = −2 (true)
4x − 3y = −11 => 4(−2) − 3(1) = −11 => −8 − 3 = −11 => −11 = −11 (true)

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: FORMS OF A LINEAR FUNCTION. There are three main forms of the equation of a linear function: standard form, slope−intercept form, and point−slope form. Study the examples shown. Standard form: ax + by = c, where a, b, and c are real numbers. For example, the linear equation 3x + 4y = 20 is in standard form. Slope–intercept form: y = mx + b, where the slope is m, and the y-intercept is (0, b). For example, the line with the equation y = −3/4 x + 5 has a slope of −3/4 and a y-intercept of (0, 5). This is the slope−intercept form of the equation 3x + 4y = 20. Point–slope form: y − k = m(x − h), where the slope is m, and (h, k) is a point on the line. For example, if the slope is −3/4 and the point (4, 2) is on the line, the equation of the line can be written y − 2 = −3/4(x − 4). You will learn more about this form in a future math course.

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: THE ELIMINATION METHOD. One method of solving systems of equations is the Elimination Method. This method involves adding both sides of two equations to eliminate a variable. Equations can be combined this way because balance is maintained when equal amounts are added to both sides of an equation. For example, if a = b and c = d, then you combine the two equations by adding and the result is a + c = b + d. This is the same result as adding equal values to each side. The first step is to rewrite the equations so that the variables are lined up vertically. Next, decide what number to multiply each equation by, if necessary, in order to make the coefficients of either of the variables sum to zero. Be sure that you can justify each step in the solution process. For example, consider the system shown: 10y − 3x = 14; 4y + 2x = −4. You can eliminate the x-terms by first multiplying the top equation by 2 and the bottom equation by 3 as shown: 2 · (10y − 3x = 14) -> 20y − 6x = 28; 3 · (4y + 2x = –4) -> 12y + 6x = −12. Then, by adding like terms in the equations, an equation with a single variable emerges that can be solved: (20y − 6x = 28) + (12y + 6x = −12) -> 32y = 16 -> y = 0.5. Finally, substitute 0.5 for y in either of the original equations to solve for x. The first equation is used here: 10(0.5) − 3x = 14 -> 5 − 3x = 14 -> −3x = 9 -> x = –3. The solution to the original system is (−3, 0.5). Check your solution by substituting it for x and y in both of the original equations and evaluating: 10(0.5) − 3(−3) = 14 -> 14 = 14 (true); 4(0.5) + 2(−3) = −4 -> −4 = −4 (true).

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: NUMBER OF SOLUTIONS TO A SYSTEM OF EQUATIONS. A system of two linear equations can have one solution, an infinite number of solutions, or no solutions. When both equations are graphed on a coordinate plane, the solution to the system of equations can be observed. If the lines intersect (that is, if they cross each other) once, there is one solution to the system of equations at the point of intersection. In the following example, the solution is (3, 1). If the lines coincide (that is, if they are the same), the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions. Coinciding lines appear to be one line because they have the same slope and the same y-intercept. In the following example, the two lines intersect each other at all points on the line. If the lines never intersect (that is, if they are parallel), there is no solution to the system of equations. Notice that the lines in the following example have the same slope but different y-intercepts, and therefore never intersect.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
TYPES OF SEQUENCES
An arithmetic sequence is a sequence with an addition (or subtraction) sequence generator. The number added to each term to get the next term is called the common difference.
A geometric sequence is a sequence with a multiplication (or division) generator. The number multiplied by each term to get the next term is called the common ratio or the multiplier.
A multiplier can also be used to increase or decrease by a given percentage. For example, the multiplier for a 7% increase is 1.07. The multiplier for a 7% decrease is 0.93.
A recursive sequence is a sequence in which each term depends on the term(s) before it. The equation of a recursive sequence requires at least one term to be specified. A recursive sequence can be arithmetic, geometric, or neither.
For example, the sequence −1, 2, 5, 26, 677, … can be defined by the recursive equation:
f(1) = −1, f(n + 1) = (f(n))2 + 1

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

INTERPRETING SLOPE AND y-INTERCEPT OF A LINEAR MODEL

A trend line and its equation provide a linear model that summarizes the association between two variables and enables you to make predictions. The slope of a linear model is the predicted change in the dependent variable (Δy) when the change in the independent variable (Δx) is 1 unit. When describing the slope of a linear model, always acknowledge that you are making a prediction, as opposed to knowing the actual value, by using words like "predict," "expect," or "estimate."

The y-intercept of a linear model is the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero. In statistical scatter plots, the vertical axis is not always drawn at the origin, so you may need to use the equation of the linear model to determine the y-intercept rather than looking at where the line crosses the vertical axis on the graph.

Also be careful about extrapolating the model too far—that is, making predictions that are far smaller or larger than the data values. Models can be valid within the range of the data, but the farther you go outside this range, the less reliable the predictions become.

When describing a linear association, you can use the slope, whether it is positive or negative, and its interpretation in context, to describe the direction of the association. For example, refer to the scatter plot of data about the weight of a car in thousands of pounds (x) and the fuel efficiency of the car in miles per gallon (y). The linear association is negative. The linear model shown has the equation y = 76 − 7.7x. The slope of −7.7 means that for every change in the weight by 1,000 pounds, the fuel efficiency is predicted to change by −7.7 miles per gallon.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

RESIDUALS
A residual measures how far a prediction made by a model is from the actual observed value:
residual = actual − predicted

A residual has the same units as the dependent variable (on the y-axis). A residual can be graphed with a vertical segment that extends from the point to the graph of the linear model (or nonlinear model). The length of this segment is the positive value of the residual. A positive residual means that the actual value is greater than the predicted value; a negative residual means that the actual value is less than the predicted value.

For example, in the graph shown, the model predicts that the net weight of cereal in a box made from 260 in2 of cardboard will be 466 grams. The negative residual of −111 grams means that the actual weight is 466 − 111 = 355 grams.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

LEAST-SQUARES REGRESSION LINE

There are two main reasons for using a line to model scattered data that appears to show a linear association. First, it describes the overall trend without listing every point. Second, it predicts values for which actual data is not available.

While many trend lines can have residuals that add up to zero, the least-squares regression line (LSRL), y = b + mx, is the unique line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals. In the diagrams shown, each dot is a data point, and the vertical line segment connecting to the regression line shows its residual. Each square has an area that represents the squared residual for its corresponding point. The LSRL is chosen to make the total area of all of these boxes as small as possible, while also making the sum of the positive and negative residuals equal to zero. Calculators and computer software can efficiently calculate the parameters of the equation, b and m.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

RESIDUAL PLOTS

A residual plot is created in order to analyze the appropriateness of a linear model. A residual plot has an x-axis that is the same as the independent variable for the data. The y-axis of a residual plot is the residual for each point. Recall that residuals have the same units as the dependent variable of the data.

The residuals are calculated by subtracting the predicted values from the actual values. The form of the residual plot is then created using these differences, plotted using the same domain as the original scatter plot.

When a linear model is a poor fit, this is often evident in the residual plot. For example, if the actual association is curved, the data points will lie above the regression line for one section, below the line for another section, and then above again, or vice versa. This same curved pattern will appear in the residual plot. The residual plot reveals that the linear model is not the best model for the data.

Instead, the residual plot should show no clear pattern; the residual points should be randomly scattered around zero. This random scatter indicates that a linear model appropriately describes the form of the association.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

CORRELATION COEFFICIENT

When describing a linear association, it is useful to know how closely data points are scattered around the LSRL. The correlation coefficient, r, provides a measure of the direction and strength of an association. This measure does not have units, so it is a useful way to compare the strength between different linear relationships, regardless of the units of the variables.
• The correlation coefficient is always a number between −1 and 1.
• A linear relationship is stronger the closer the value of r is to −1 or 1.
• A linear relationship is weaker the closer the value of r is to 0.
• If r = 1 or r = −1, the association is perfectly linear. The points lie exactly on the LSRL.
• When r is positive, the direction of the linear association is positive.
• When r is negative, the direction of the linear association is negative.

paragraph:
NONLINEAR MODELS
For some data sets, a nonlinear model fits the data better and makes better predictions than a linear model. This can often be determined by comparing the residual plots of various models.
Sometimes the physical situation can provide clues about the type of model to use. When dealing with dry-ice sublimation, an exponential model makes physical sense because the quantity being measured decays over time.
A quadratic model would not have been very effective because of its U-shape, which implies that the process will reverse at some point. On the other hand, if predictions were being made about the path of a projectile, such as a ball being thrown, a quadratic model of the data would make sense because the object will return to the ground after it reaches its peak height.
The models used for this course are:
Linear: y = b + ax
Exponential: y = abˣ
Quadratic: y = ax² + bx + c
Recall that the correlation coefficient, r, can only measure the strength of linear models.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: GRAPHS WITH ASYMPTOTES

A mathematically clear and complete definition of an asymptote requires some ideas from Calculus, but some examples of graphs with asymptotes might help you recognize them when they occur. In the examples provided, the dotted lines are the asymptotes. In the two lowest graphs, the vertical axis, x = 0, is also an asymptote.

Asymptotes can be diagonal lines or even curves. In this course, asymptotes will almost always be horizontal or vertical lines. The graph of a function has a horizontal asymptote if, as you trace along the graph out to the left or right (that is, as you choose x-coordinates farther and farther away from zero, either toward infinity or toward negative infinity), the distance between the graph of the function and the asymptote gets closer to zero.

A graph has a vertical asymptote if, as you choose values of x closer and closer to a certain value, from either the left or right (or both), f(x) gets farther away from zero, either toward infinity or toward negative infinity.

If two expressions are equal only for certain values of the variable, they can form an equation that is considered to be sometimes true. For example, x + 2 is equal to 3x − 8 only when x = 5, so the equation x + 2 = 3x − 8 is said to be sometimes true.

If two expressions are not equal for any value of the variable, they can form an equation that is considered to be never true. For example, x − 5 is not equal to x + 1 for any value of x, so the equation x − 5 = x + 1 is said to be never true.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: COMPOUND INTEREST

A bank can pay simple interest, in which case, the amount in the bank grows linearly. For example, 3% simple interest accrued annually on an initial investment of $2,500 would grow in a sequence with a common difference: 0.03(2,500) = $75. The equation for this is f(n) = 2,500 + 75n, where n represents the number of years and f(n) represents the money in the bank. A table for this situation follows.
Time (Years): 0, 1, 2, 3, 10
Money in Bank ($): 2,500.00, 2,575.00, 2,650.00, 2,725.00, 3,250.00

If the bank compounds interest, the relationship is exponential. For example, 3% annual interest, compounded annually, would have a constant percent rate of growth of 1.03 every year. The equation for this is r(n) = 2,500 · 1.03^n, where n represents the number of years and r(n) represents the money in the bank.
Time (Years): 0, 1, 2, 3, 10
Money in Bank ($): 2,500.00, 2,575.00, 2,652.25, 2,731.82, 3,359.79
Note that dollar amounts are rounded to the nearest cent.

If the bank compounds monthly, the 3% annual interest becomes (3% / year) / (12 months / year) = 0.25% per month, and the constant percent rate of growth becomes 1.0025. The equation for this is q(m) = 2,500 · 1.0025^m, where m represents the number of months and q(m) represents the money in the bank (in dollars). A table for this situation follows.
Time (Years): 0, 12, 24, 36, 120
Money in Bank ($): 2,500.00, 2,576.04, 2,654.39, 2,735.13, 3,373.38
Note that dollar amounts are rounded to the nearest cent.

7-47. HALF-LIFE
Radiometric dating is a scientific technique used to determine the age of objects, such as rocks or artifacts. It takes advantage of the fact that these objects contain rare isotopes of certain elements, which decay at stable rates. paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS
An exponential function is a function of the form f(x) = ab^x where b > 0, b ≠ 1, and a ≠ 0. Note that the variable x is the exponent. All exponential functions of this form have the x-axis as an asymptote because f(x) ≠ 0.
The coefficient a is the y-intercept. For example, a = 3 for the function f(x) = 3 · 2^x. Therefore, in the table and graph of f(x) = 3 · 2^x shown, (0, 3) is the y-intercept.
The base b is the constant percent rate of change. For each additional unit of the x-value, the previous value of f(x) is multiplied by b. For example, in the table shown, the constant percent rate of change is 2.
For values of b > 1, the value of the function increases as x increases, and this is “exponential growth.” When 0 < b < 1, the value of the function decreases as x increases, and this is “exponential decay.”
A common application of exponential decay is half-life. Half-life is the amount of time it takes for half the original amount to remain. In problem 7-47, you saw that the half-life of uranium-235 is 704 million years. That is, it takes 704 million years until half the original amount of uranium-235 remains (no matter how much you started with).
Geometric sequences are a special case of exponential functions in which the domain is restricted to the positive integers.

NEGATIVE AND FRACTIONAL EXPONENTS
Property: x⁰ = 1 for x ≠ 0
Examples: 2⁰ = 1, (−3)⁰ = 1, (1/4)⁰ = 1

Property: x⁻ⁿ = 1/(xⁿ) for x ≠ 0
Examples: x⁻³ = 1/(x³), y⁻⁴ = 1/(y⁴), 4⁻² = 1/(4²) = 1/16, (−4)⁻⁶ = 1/((−4)⁶) = 1/4,096

Examples: 1/(x⁻⁵) = x⁵, 1/(x⁻²) = x², 1/(3⁻²) = 3² = 9, 1/((−2)⁻⁵) = (−2)⁵ = −32

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
EQUATIONS FOR SEQUENCES
ARITHMETIC SEQUENCES
The equation for an arithmetic sequence is f(n) = mn + b, where n is the term number, m is the sequence generator (the common difference), and b is the zeroth term. Compare these equations to a continuous linear function f(x) = mx + b, where m is the growth (slope) and b is the starting value (y-intercept).
For example, the arithmetic sequence 4, 7, 10, 13, … could be represented by f(n) = 3n + 1. (Note that “4” is the first term of this sequence, so “1” is the zeroth term.)
Another way to write the equation of an arithmetic sequence is to use the first term in the equation, as in f(n) = m(n − 1) + f(1), where f(1) is the first term. The sequence in the example could be represented by f(n) = 3(n − 1) + 4.
You could even write an equation using any other term in the sequence. The equation using the fourth term in the example would be f(n) = 3(n − 4) + 13.
GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
The equation for a geometric sequence is f(n) = ab^n, where n is the term number, b is the sequence generator (the multiplier or common ratio), and a is the zeroth term. Compare these equations to a continuous exponential function f(x) = ab^x, where b is the growth (multiplier) and a is the starting value (y-intercept).
For example, the geometric sequence 6, 18, 54, … could be represented by f(n) = 2 · 3^n.
You can write a first-term form of the equation for a geometric sequence as well: f(n) = f(1) · b^(n − 1). For example, the first-term form would be f(n) = 6 · 3^(n − 1).

paragraph: Methods & Meanings: MORE VOCABULARY FOR EXPRESSIONS. Since algebraic expressions can be written in several different forms, there are special words used to help describe these expressions. For example, if the expression can be written in the form ax^2 + bx + c and if a is not 0, it is called a quadratic expression. Review the following examples of quadratic expressions: x^2 - 15x + 26, 16m^2 - 25, 12 - 3k^2 + 5k. The way an expression is written can also be named. When an expression is written in product form, it is said to be factored. When factored, each of the expressions being multiplied is called a factor. For example, the factored form of x^2 - 15x + 26 is (x - 13)(x - 2), so x - 13 and x - 2 are each factors of the original expression. Finally, if the expression is a polynomial (see the Methods & Meanings box in Lesson 3.2.3), the number of terms can help you name the polynomial. If the polynomial has one term, it is called a monomial, while a polynomial with two terms is called a binomial. If the polynomial has three terms, it is called a trinomial. Review the following examples. • Monomials: 15y^2 and -2 • Binomials: 16m - 25 and 7h^9 + 1/2 • Trinomials: 12 - 3k^3 + 5k and x^2 - 15x + 26

paragraph: Methods & Meanings - ZERO PRODUCT PROPERTY. When the product of two or more numbers is zero, one of those numbers must be zero. This is known as the Zero Product Property. This property can be written as follows: If a and b are two numbers where a · b = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0. For example, if (2x − 3)(x + 5) = 0, then 2x − 3 = 0 or x + 5 = 0. Solving yields the solutions x = 3/2 or x = −5. This property helps you solve quadratic equations when the equation can be written as a product of factors.

paragraph: 8-100. COMPLETING THE SQUARE. Jessica was at home struggling with her Algebra homework. She had missed class and did not understand the new method called completing the square. paragraph: Methods & Meanings: THE QUADRATIC FORMULA. Why does x = (-b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a) give the solutions of ax^2 + bx + c = 0? One way to derive this formula is to rewrite the standard form of a quadratic equation in a factorable form and solve for x. This process is shown. Begin with the quadratic equation in standard form, then multiply each side by 4a: ax^2 + bx + c = 0; 4a(ax^2 + bx + c) = (0)4a; 4a^2 x^2 + 4abx + 4ac = 0. Add b^2 − 4ac to each side to get a perfect square trinomial: 4a^2 x^2 + 4abx + b^2 = b^2 − 4ac. Factor the left side of the equation: (2ax + b)^2 = b^2 − 4ac. Take the square root of each side. Use absolute value to calculate the positive and negative values for 2ax + b, then solve for x: √( (2ax + b)^2 ) = √(b^2 − 4ac); |2ax + b| = √(b^2 − 4ac). 2ax + b = √(b^2 − 4ac) gives 2ax = −b + √(b^2 − 4ac), so x = (−b + √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). −(2ax + b) = √(b^2 − 4ac) or 2ax + b = −√(b^2 − 4ac) gives 2ax = −b − √(b^2 − 4ac), so x = (−b − √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). Finally, use the ± sign to write the formula as a single equation: x = (-b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). Notice that a cannot equal zero because you cannot divide by 0! However, if a = 0, then this equation would not be quadratic and you would not use this formula.

Methods & Meanings: SOLVING A QUADRATIC EQUATION
So far in this course, you have learned three algebraic methods to solve a quadratic equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Each of the following examples demonstrates one of the methods.

EXAMPLE 1: Solve 3x^2 + x − 14 = 0 for x using factoring and the Zero Product Property.
First, make sure the quadratic expression is equal to 0. Then, factor the quadratic so it is written as a product: (3x + 7)(x − 2) = 0.
The Zero Product Property states that if the product of two terms is 0, then at least one of the factors must be 0. Thus, 3x + 7 = 0 or x − 2 = 0. Solving each equation for x reveals that x = -7/3 or x = 2. This method only works when the quadratic can be factored.

(x + 2.5)^2 = 2.25
|x + 2.5| = √2.25
x + 2.5 = 1.5 => x = -1
-(x + 2.5) = 1.5 => x = -4
The solution is x = −1 or x = −4.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: REWRITING SQUARE ROOTS
Before calculators were readily available, people found it convenient to rewrite square root expressions to make it easier to perform calculations and compare them. A square root can be rewritten so there are no perfect square factors (such as 4, 25, and 81) under the radical symbol. The rewritten form is sometimes called simplified radical form. Here are some examples of this process.

EXAMPLE 1: Rewrite √45 without any perfect square factors under the radical symbol.
First rewrite √45 in an equivalent factored form so that one of the factors is a perfect square. Then take the square root of the perfect square.
√45 = √(9 · 5) = √9 · √5 = 3√5

EXAMPLE 2: Rewrite √72 without any perfect square factors under the radical symbol.
Note that √72 can be rewritten as √36 · √2, as √9 · √8, or as √4 · √18. You will get the same result after you complete the process of factoring out perfect squares.
√72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2
√72 = √9 · √8 = 3√(4 · 2) = 3√4 · √2 = 3 · 2√2 = 6√2
√72 = √4 · √18 = 2√(9 · 2) = 2√9 · √2 = 2 · 3√2 = 6√2

When you take the square root of an integer that is not a perfect square, the result is a decimal that never repeats itself and never ends. It is a number that cannot be written as a fraction using only integers. This result is called an irrational number. The irrational numbers and the rational numbers together form the real numbers.

Generally, when a decimal approximation of an irrational square root is desired, you will use a calculator. However, for an exact answer, called exact form or radical form, the number must be written using the √ symbol. For example, √45 and 3√5 are in exact form, and 6.71 is a decimal approximation.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: CURVE FITTING AN EXPONENTIAL FUNCTION
To write an exponential function that goes through two points, create a system of equations by substituting one (x, y) point into y = ab^x, then substituting the other point. Rewrite both equations in “a =” form. Solve the system with the Equal Values Method to determine a and b, and now you can write the equation.
For example, write an exponential function that passes through (2, 14) and (5, 112). Create a system of equations by substituting (x, y) = (2, 14) into y = ab^x, and then substituting again with (x, y) = (5, 112):
14 = ab^2 => a = 14/b^2
112 = ab^5 => a = 112/b^5
Use the Equal Values Method to determine b:
14/b^2 = 112/b^5
14b^5 = 112b^2
14 · b^5/b^2 = 112
14b^3 = 112
b^3 = 112/14
b^3 = 8
b = 2
Use either original equation to determine a:
b = 2
14 = ab^2
14 = a(2)^2
14 = 4a
14/4 = a
3.5 = a
The equation of the exponential function that passes through the two given points is y = 3.5 · 2^x.

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: SOLVING ONE-VARIABLE LINEAR INEQUALITIES. To solve a one-variable linear inequality, change the inequality to an equation and solve for x. The solution to the equation is the boundary point of the inequality. For example, x = 12 is the boundary point for the inequality 10 − 2(x − 3) ≥ −8, as shown: 10 − 2(x − 3) ≥ −8; 10 − 2(x − 3) = −8; 10 − 2x + 6 = −8; −2x + 16 = −8; −2x = −24; x = 12. Since the original inequality is true when x = 12, place your boundary point on the number line as a solid point. (When the inequality is < or >, the boundary point is not included in the answer and is indicated with an open circle at the boundary point.) Then test one value on either side of the boundary point in the original inequality to determine which set of numbers makes the inequality true. Testing x = 8: 10 − 2(8 − 3) ≥ −8 => 0 ≥ −8 (true). Testing x = 15: 10 − 2(15 − 3) ≥ −8 => −14 ≥ −8 (false). Since x = 8 produces a true statement, the region on the number line containing x = 8 is the solution, or x ≤ 12.

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: SOLVING INEQUALITIES WITH TWO VARIABLES. To represent the solutions to an inequality with two variables, first graph the boundary line or curve. If the inequality does not include an equality (that is, if it is > or < rather than ≥ or ≤), then the graph of the boundary is dashed to indicate that it is not included in the solution. Otherwise, the boundary is a solid line or curve. Once the boundary is graphed, choose a point that does not lie on the boundary to test (substitute) in the inequality. If that point makes the inequality true, then the entire region in which that point lies consists of the solution. As an example, for the inequality y < −2/3 x + 2, the first step is to graph the equation y = −2/3 x + 2 with a dashed line to indicate that the line is not included in the solution. Then, test the coordinates of a point that is not on the boundary line in the inequality. The point (0, 0) is chosen and substituted into the inequality: at (0, 0), x = 0 and y = 0, y < −2/3 x + 2 => 0 < −2/3(0) + 2 => 0 < 2 (true). Since the inequality is true, shade the region where (0, 0) is located, as shown in the graph. All points in the shaded region are solutions. For y ≥ x^2 − 4, the boundary curve is solid since the inequality includes an equality. The curve y = x^2 − 4 is shown, and the point (0, 0) can be tested: 0 ≥ (0)^2 − 4 => 0 ≥ −4 (true). The inequality is true, so the region that includes (0, 0) is shaded. Note that there are infinitely many points that are solutions to each of the inequalities.

paragraph:
Throughout this course, you studied different types of equations and inequalities, including linear equations and inequalities, quadratic equations, and systems of equations and inequalities. You also experimented with a variety of methods to solve those equations and inequalities.

In Chapter 10, you will extend your solving skills to include other types of equations, including equations with square roots, absolute values, variables in exponents, and messy fractions. Then you will learn how to determine the number of possible solutions for an equation without actually solving it. You will also consider “imaginary” solutions to quadratic equations.

This chapter also focuses on intersections of functions. You will learn how to use the intersection of the graphs of two functions to determine the solution to an equation. Then you will solve quadratic and absolute value inequalities.

Although much of this chapter focuses on solving equations, you will also determine whether there is an association between two categorical variables that are represented on a two-way table.

In Chapter 10, you will build on all of the major conceptual ideas of this math course.

TWO-WAY TABLE VOCABULARY

Mathematicians often display the relationships between two categorical variables in a two-way table such as the one shown. In the example, one variable is whether the student is an athlete or not, and the other variable is the student’s class level.

When entries in the table are frequencies (counts), mathematicians refer to the table as a frequency table. They refer to the entries in a two-way table as joint frequencies. The sum of a row or column on a frequency table is the marginal frequency or marginal distribution.

In the two-way table shown, the joint frequency of 12th grade athletes is 49 students, and the marginal frequency of 9th grade athletes is 103 students.

A relative frequency is a percent (or proportion) of some subgroup, as opposed to a count. The conditional relative frequency of being a non-athlete, given that you are in 11th grade, is 68/108 ≈ 63%.

paragraph:
EQUIVALENT EQUATIONS

Two equations are equivalent if all of their solutions are the same. There are several ways to transform one equation into a different, yet equivalent, equation. Common ways include:
• adding the same number to both sides;
• subtracting the same number from both sides;
• multiplying both sides by the same (non-zero) number;
• dividing both sides by the same (non-zero) number; and
• rewriting one or both sides of the equation.

For example, the following equations are equivalent to 2x + 1 = 3.
20x + 10 = 30
2(x + 0.5) = 3
2x/3 + 1/3 = 1
0.002x + 0.001 = 0.003

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: SOLVING EQUATIONS WITH FRACTIONS (ALSO KNOWN AS FRACTION BUSTERS)
Example: Solve x/3 + x/5 = 2 for x.
This equation would be much easier to solve if it had no fractions. Therefore, the first goal is to write an equivalent equation that has no fractions.
To eliminate the denominators, multiply both sides of the equation by a common denominator. In this example, the lowest common denominator of x/3 and x/5 is 15, so multiplying both sides of the equation by 15 eliminates the fractions. Another approach is to multiply both sides of the equation by one denominator and then by the other. Either way, the result is an equivalent equation without fractions.
The number used to eliminate the denominators is called a Fraction Buster. Now, the equation resembles many you have seen before, and you can solve it in the usual way.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: METHODS TO SOLVE SINGLE-VARIABLE EQUATIONS
Here are three different methods you can use to solve single-variable equations.

REWRITING
Use algebraic techniques to rewrite the equation. This often involves using the Distributive Property to eliminate parentheses. Then solve the equation using the solution methods you know.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5x - 5 = 15
  5x = 20
  x = 4

LOOKING INSIDE
Choose a part of the equation that includes the variable and is grouped together by parentheses or another symbol. Make sure it includes all occurrences of the variable. Ask yourself, "What must this part of the equation equal to make the equation true?" Use that information to write and solve a new, equivalent equation that you can solve in fewer steps.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5(?) = 15
  ? = 3
  (x - 1) = 3
  x = 4

UNDOING
Start by undoing the last operation performed on the variable. This will give you an equivalent equation that can be solved in fewer steps, which you can solve either by undoing the process again or with another approach.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5(x - 1)/5 = 15/5
  x - 1 = 3
  x = 4

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: FORMS OF A QUADRATIC EQUATION
There are three main forms of a quadratic function: standard form, factored form, and graphing form (see the Methods & Meanings box in Lesson 8.2.4). Similarly, there are three forms of a single-variable quadratic equation.
Standard form: Any quadratic equation written in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
Factored form: Any quadratic equation written in the form a(x + b)(x + c) = 0.
Perfect Square form: Any quadratic equation written in the form (ax − b)^2 = c^2. Notice that when you build the expression on the left side of the equation shown with tiles, it forms a perfect square. For example, for the equation (2x + 3)^2 = 5, the equation could be represented as shown.
Solutions to a quadratic equation can be written in exact form (radical form). For example, x = (-3 + sqrt(5))/2 or x = (-3 - sqrt(5))/2.
Alternatively, solutions can be estimated in approximate decimal form. For example, x ≈ −0.38 or x ≈ −2.62.

Methods & Meanings: THE NUMBER SYSTEM
The collection (set) of all numbers can be organized into categories.
• COMPLEX NUMBERS (for example, 3 + i, 4 - 7i)
  - IMAGINARY NUMBERS (for example, i, sqrt(-49), 4/13 i, πi, i*sqrt(2)). There are many subcategories of imaginary numbers.
  - REAL NUMBERS
    * IRRATIONAL NUMBERS (non-repeating decimals; for example, sqrt(5), -sqrt(2), π, e)
    * RATIONAL NUMBERS (quotients of integers)
      ~ FRACTIONS (repeating and terminating decimals; for example, 1/2, -1/27, -2.333..., 0.25, 2.175656...)
      ~ INTEGERS
        + NEGATIVE INTEGERS (for example, -1, -9, -107)
        + WHOLE NUMBERS

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: SOLVING ABSOLUTE VALUE EQUATIONS. To algebraically solve an equation with an absolute value, first isolate the absolute value on one side of the equation. 5|2x − 3| − 6 = 29, 5|2x − 3| = 35, |2x − 3| = 7. Note that you cannot distribute over an absolute value. For example, 5|2x − 3| ≠ 5(2x) − 5(3). Determine the possible values of the quantity inside the absolute value. Since |2x − 3| = 7, then the quantity (2x − 3) must be 7 away from 0, or located at either 7 or −7. With these two values, set up new equations and solve as shown: (2x − 3) = 7 gives 2x = 10, x = 5; -(2x − 3) = 7 gives 2x − 3 = −7, 2x = −4, x = −2. To check your solutions, substitute each value back into the original equation and evaluate.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings - NUMBER OF SOLUTIONS TO A QUADRATIC EQUATION: The solutions to a quadratic equation written in standard form, ax^2 + bx + c = 0, are x = (-b ± √(b^2 − 4ac))/(2a). You can tell how many solutions a quadratic equation in standard form has by looking at the value of the expression b^2 − 4ac. This expression, b^2 − 4ac, is called the discriminant. • If b^2 − 4ac is negative, there are no real solutions, because the square roots of negative numbers are not real numbers. However, there are two complex solutions when b^2 − 4ac is negative. • If b^2 − 4ac is zero, there is only one solution, because 0 = 0. • If b^2 − 4ac is positive, there are two solutions: x = (-b + √(b^2 − 4ac))/(2a) and x = (-b − √(b^2 − 4ac))/(2a). If a quadratic is written as a perfect square, (px − q)^2 = r, solve by taking the square root of both sides: p − q = ±√r. The number of solutions is determined by r. • If r is negative, there are no real solutions. • If r is zero, there is one solution. • If r is positive, there are two solutions. If a quadratic is in factored form, a(x + m)(x + n) = 0, use the Zero Product Property to solve: x + m = 0 and x + n = 0. If m = n, then there is only one solution.

reasoning: This is a standard expository reference box explaining the discriminant and the number of solutions for a quadratic equation. It contains no error-focused pedagogy or warnings about mistakes.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings - INTERQUARTILE RANGE AND BOX PLOTS: Quartiles are points that divide a data set into four equal parts. (Notice how the word “quartile” begins with “quar,” just like other words such as “quarter” that also have something to do with the number four.) One of these points is the median of the whole data set. The first quartile (Q1) is the median of the lower half, and the third quartile (Q3) is the median of the upper half. To determine the quartiles, the data set must be ordered from smallest to largest. Note that if there are an odd number of data values, the median is not included in either half of the data set. Suppose you have the data set: 22, 43, 14, 7, 2, 32, 9, 36, and 12. The interquartile range (IQR) is the difference between the third and first quartiles. It is used to measure the spread (the variability) of the middle 50% of the data. The interquartile range is 34 − 8 = 26. A box plot (also known as a box-and-whisker plot) displays a five-number summary of data: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile, and the maximum. The box contains “the middle half” of the data and visually displays the size of the IQR. The right segment represents the top 25% of the data, and the left segment represents the bottom 25% of the data. A box plot makes it easy to see where the data is spread out and where it is concentrated. The wider the box, the more the data is spread out. Often, a box plot is placed above a histogram to create a combination histogram and box plot. These two representations would use the same x-axis scale. An example is shown.

11-63. STANDARD DEVIATION
In Chapter 6, you learned about residuals—the distance that points are from the LSRL. In the process of determining the LSRL, you had to ensure that all the residuals were positive because distances are positive. You learned that statisticians prefer to make numbers positive by squaring them, rather than using the absolute value.

3. Calculate the average squared distance.
4. Take the square root of the average squared distance.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: DESCRIBING SPREAD OF A DATA DISTRIBUTION
Data distributions can be summarized by describing their center, shape, spread, and outliers. You have learned three ways to describe the spread.
INTERQUARTILE RANGE (IQR)
The variability, or spread, in the distribution can be numerically summarized with the interquartile range (IQR). The IQR is calculated by subtracting the first quartile from the third quartile. The IQR is the range of the middle half of the data. IQR can represent the spread of any data distribution, even if the distribution is not symmetric or contains outliers.
STANDARD DEVIATION
Either the interquartile range or standard deviation can be used to represent the spread if the data distribution is symmetric and contains no outliers. The standard deviation is the square root of the average of the squares of the distances from the mean.
For example, consider the following data set (in kilograms).
10, 12, 14, 16, 18
• The mean is 14 kg.
• The distances of each data value to the mean are: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4 kg.
• The distances squared are: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16 kg^2.
• The mean of the squared distances is 8 kg^2.
• The square root is 2.83. Therefore, the standard deviation is 2.83 kg.
RANGE
The range (maximum minus minimum) is usually not a very effective way to describe the spread, as it considers only the extreme values rather than how the bulk of the data is distributed.

paragraph:
Review

Modeling scattered data with a trend line (or a nonlinear function) is a way to describe the trend of the data without listing every data point. The model can also be used to make predictions about points where actual data is not available.

When describing an association between two variables, the form, direction, strength, and outliers should be described.

The form can be linear or curved, and it can contain clusters or have gaps. Residual plots can help determine whether a particular type of model is appropriate.

The direction is positive if one variable increases as the other variable increases, and negative if one variable decreases as the other increases. If there is no apparent pattern in the scatter plot, then the variables have no association. When describing a linear association, you can use the slope and its numerical interpretation in context to describe the direction of the association.

The strength describes how closely the data points cluster around the line or curve of best fit. An association is strong when there is very little scatter about the model of best fit, and weak when there is a lot of scatter. For a linear association, the correlation coefficient r can be used to numerically describe and interpret the strength.

Outliers are data points that are far removed from the rest of the data.

A residual measures how far a prediction made by a model is from the actual observed value: residual = actual – predicted. Residuals have the same units as the dependent variable (the y-axis). A positive residual means that the actual value is greater than the predicted value; a negative residual means that the actual value is less than the predicted value. A residual plot is a graphical representation of the residuals, with the x-axis representing the independent variable and the y-axis representing the residual values. If the points in a residual plot are randomly scattered around zero, the model is a good fit for the data. If the residuals show a pattern, such as forming a curve or trend, the model may not be appropriate because it does not capture the true relationship between the variables.

A consistent linear model for data can be found by determining the line that makes the sum of the squares of the residuals as small as possible. This line is called the least-squares regression line (LSRL). Graphing technology can quickly determine the LSRL.

The correlation coefficient, r, is a measure of the strength and direction of a linear association between two variables. The value of the correlation coefficient is always between –1 and 1. Values of r close to 1 or −1 indicate that the data points lie close to the LSRL, showing a stronger linear association. Values closer to 0 indicate that the data points are very scattered, indicating a weak association. A positive correlation coefficient indicates an increasing trend (positive slope), while a negative correlation coefficient indicates a decreasing trend (negative slope). A correlation coefficient near 0 indicates no linear association between the variables, though the data may still exhibit a nonlinear pattern.
